interactions.label: A patient with a large ventricular septal defect develops progressive cyanosis,

params.question: A patient with a large ventricular septal defect develops progressive cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythaemia over several years. Why is surgical closure of the VSD now contraindicated?

answers.text: The VSD has become too large and fibrotic to close surgically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VSD size is not the barrier. The contraindication arises from irreversible pulmonary vascular disease — medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis graded at Heath-Edwards grade 4 and beyond.

answers.text: Irreversible pulmonary vascular changes mean the VSD now serves as the right ventricle's only pressure outlet

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At Heath-Edwards grade 4+, pulmonary vascular remodelling is irreversible. The VSD lets the right ventricle decompress against fixed pulmonary hypertension. Closing it would cause acute right heart failure.

answers.text: The right ventricle has atrophied and cannot generate adequate pressure after closure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In Eisenmenger syndrome, the right ventricle is hypertrophied (not atrophied) from chronic pressure overload. The issue is irreversible pulmonary vascular resistance, not right ventricular weakness.

answers.text: Closing the defect would cause acute left ventricular volume overload

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The shunt has already reversed to right-to-left, so the left ventricle is not volume-overloaded. The danger is to the right ventricle, which would lose its only decompression pathway against fixed pulmonary hypertension.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Eisenmenger syndrome, chronic volume overload from the left-to-right shunt causes irreversible pulmonary vascular remodelling (Heath-Edwards grade 4+). The shunt reverses to right-to-left, and the VSD becomes the right ventricle's only pressure outlet. Surgical closure would remove that outlet, causing right heart failure.
Well done. Eisenmenger syndrome reverses the shunt direction once pulmonary vascular resistance becomes irreversible, making the VSD a lifeline for the right ventricle.

interactions.label: Which pairing correctly distinguishes dilated cardiomyopathy from hypertrophic c

params.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes dilated cardiomyopathy from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

answers.text: DCM causes diastolic failure with thick walls; HCM causes systolic failure with thin walls

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two. DCM causes systolic failure with thin, flabby walls and four-chamber enlargement, while HCM causes diastolic failure with a thickened interventricular septum.

answers.text: DCM causes systolic failure with four-chamber enlargement; HCM causes diastolic failure with asymmetric septal hypertrophy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DCM produces thin, dilated ventricles that cannot contract effectively (systolic failure). HCM thickens the septum asymmetrically, reducing compliance and obstructing outflow (diastolic failure). HCM is also the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

answers.text: DCM is driven by sarcomere mutations; HCM is driven by titin and lamin mutations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The genetic causes are reversed. Sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3) drive HCM. Titin and lamin mutations are associated with DCM.

answers.text: DCM presents as sudden death in young athletes; HCM presents as chronic progressive heart failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HCM, not DCM, is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes due to myofibre disarray creating electrical instability. DCM typically presents with progressive heart failure and is the leading indication for cardiac transplantation.

overallFeedback.feedback: DCM = thin, dilated heart, systolic failure, titin/lamin mutations. HCM = thick septum, diastolic failure, sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3), myofibre disarray, and the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes.
Excellent. Remembering this functional distinction — systolic (DCM) versus diastolic (HCM) failure — helps predict clinical presentations and guides management.

interactions.label: In acute rheumatic fever, Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci directly invade t

params.question: In acute rheumatic fever, Group A beta-haemolytic streptococci directly invade the heart and cause tissue destruction.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. In rheumatic fever, no streptococci invade the heart. The mechanism is molecular mimicry: antibodies raised against the streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins. The immune system — through Type II and Type IV hypersensitivity — does all the damage.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. No bacteria enter the heart in rheumatic fever. The damage is entirely immune-mediated: antibodies against streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins (Type II hypersensitivity), amplified by T-cell responses (Type IV hypersensitivity).

interactions.label: In infective endocarditis, Osler nodes and Janeway lesions arise from different

params.question: In infective endocarditis, Osler nodes and Janeway lesions arise from different pathogenic mechanisms. Which statement correctly explains this difference?

answers.text: Osler nodes are caused by septic emboli and are painless; Janeway lesions are caused by immune complexes and are tender

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two. Osler nodes are TENDER and immune complex-mediated. Janeway lesions are PAINLESS and caused by septic emboli.

answers.text: Osler nodes result from immune complex deposition and are tender; Janeway lesions result from septic emboli and are painless

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Osler nodes (tender fingertip nodules) and Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages) are both immune complex-mediated. Janeway lesions (painless haemorrhagic palmar spots) result from septic emboli lodging in dermal vessels.

answers.text: Both are caused by septic emboli but differ in size and location

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Their mechanisms are fundamentally different. Osler nodes arise from immune complex deposition (tender, fingertips), while Janeway lesions arise from septic embolisation (painless, palms).

answers.text: Both are caused by immune complex deposition but Osler nodes occur only in acute IE and Janeway lesions only in subacute IE

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osler nodes are immune complex-mediated, but Janeway lesions are embolic — the mechanisms differ. Neither is restricted to one form of endocarditis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Osler nodes = TENDER, fingertips, immune complex deposition. Janeway lesions = PAINLESS, palms, septic emboli. Roth spots in the retina share the immune complex mechanism with Osler nodes.
Well done. The tender (immune complex) versus painless (septic embolic) distinction maps directly to the underlying pathogenic mechanism — a useful clinical discriminator.

interactions.label: A patient with pericardial effusion presents with hypotension, distended neck ve

params.question: A patient with pericardial effusion presents with hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. Which additional finding confirms cardiac tamponade?

answers.text: A loud pericardial friction rub on auscultation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A friction rub is characteristic of fibrinous pericarditis, typically heard before significant effusion develops. As fluid accumulates and separates the pericardial layers, the friction rub usually disappears.

answers.text: A systolic blood pressure fall exceeding 10 mmHg on inspiration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is pulsus paradoxus — the haemodynamic hallmark of tamponade. Inspiration increases right ventricular filling, shifting the septum leftward and reducing left ventricular output. Pericardiocentesis is the immediate treatment.

answers.text: Eggshell calcification of the pericardium on chest X-ray

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eggshell calcification indicates chronic constrictive pericarditis, not acute tamponade. Constriction follows years of scarring (commonly from tuberculosis in India), whereas tamponade is an acute haemodynamic emergency.

answers.text: Elevated serum troponin levels indicating myocardial necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Troponin elevation suggests myocardial injury (infarction or myocarditis), not tamponade. Tamponade is extrinsic compression of the heart by fluid, confirmed by pulsus paradoxus and echocardiography.

overallFeedback.feedback: The triad described (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) is Beck's triad. Pulsus paradoxus — a systolic BP drop >10 mmHg on inspiration — confirms the haemodynamic compromise. Rate of fluid accumulation, not volume alone, determines tamponade risk.
Well done. Beck's triad plus pulsus paradoxus clinches the diagnosis of tamponade. Rapid pericardiocentesis is life-saving.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old woman presents with syncope that occurs on standing and resolves o

params.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with syncope that occurs on standing and resolves on lying down. Echocardiography reveals a pedunculated mass in the left atrium. Which mechanism best explains her postural symptoms?

answers.text: The tumour secretes vasoactive substances that cause orthostatic hypotension

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While myxomas can cause constitutional symptoms, the postural syncope here is mechanical. The pedunculated mass prolapses through the mitral valve in the upright position, obstructing inflow.

answers.text: Tumour fragments embolise to the cerebral circulation when she stands

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Embolisation from a myxoma's friable surface can cause stroke, but this produces fixed neurological deficits — not reversible, posture-dependent syncope.

answers.text: The pedunculated mass prolapses through the mitral valve, intermittently obstructing left ventricular filling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Myxoma arises near the fossa ovalis on a stalk. Standing allows gravity to pull it into the mitral orifice, creating a ball-valve obstruction that mimics mitral stenosis. Lying down relieves the obstruction.

answers.text: The mass compresses the pulmonary veins, reducing venous return to the left atrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A left atrial myxoma obstructs the mitral valve orifice, not the pulmonary veins. The ball-valve mechanism — mass falling into the valve when upright — produces the characteristic posture-dependent syncope.

overallFeedback.feedback: Left atrial myxoma is pedunculated, arising near the fossa ovalis. In the upright position, gravity pulls the mass through the mitral valve, obstructing filling and mimicking mitral stenosis. This ball-valve mechanism explains the posture-dependent syncope.

Excellent. Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults. Its pedunculated, gelatinous nature creates a ball-valve effect at the mitral orifice, and posture-dependent syncope is the clinical hallmark.
